Muqatil said: "a place of waiting for the enemies and a passageway for the allies." The form mif‘āl is used for both masculine and feminine without a tā’ and carries the sense of the relative (nisba), i.e., "possessing watching"; and everything that comes in reports and attributes in the sense of nisba carries the sense of intensification and permanence. Al-Azhari said: al-mirṣād is the place where the enemy is watched. Al-Hasan said: "Indeed, over Hell is a lookout: whoever comes with a passport passes, and whoever does not come with a passport is detained." Abu ‘Amr, al-Minqari and Ibn Ya‘mar read ﴿أنّ جهنم﴾ (anna jahannama) with a fatḥa on the hamza, while the majority read it with a kasra. (مَآبًا) (ma’aban): a return. ‘Abdullah, ‘Alqama, Zayd ibn ‘Ali, Ibn Thabbat, ‘Amr ibn Maymun, ‘Amr ibn Shurahbil, Talha, al-A‘mash, Hamza, Qutayba, Sawra and Rawh read ﴿لَبِثِينَ﴾ (labithina) without an alif after the lam, while the majority read it with an alif after it. Fā‘il indicates one in whom the act has occurred, and fa‘il indicates one whose nature is that, like ḥādhir and ḥadhir. (أحْقابًا) (aḥqāban): its discussion has preceded in al-Kahf at His saying: ﴿أو أمضي حقبا﴾ [al-Kahf: 60]. The meaning here is: age after age, each age followed by another without end. The word ḥuqub is used only where the succession of times is intended, as in the verse of Abu Tammam:
"Indeed, the ages have taken from the abode of Mawiyya, the ages that wear down the abandoned places, or are they plundered?"

It is permissible for ﴿للطاغين﴾ (lil-ṭāghīna) to be connected to ﴿مرصادا﴾, and it is permissible for it to be connected to (ma’aban). ﴿لابثين﴾ (lābithīna) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from ﴿الطاغين﴾, and ﴿أحقابا﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time. Al-Zamakhshari said: there is another possibility, that it be from ḥaqiba ‘āmunā when its rain and goodness diminish, and ḥaqiba when one misses sustenance, so he is ḥaqib, and its plural is aḥqāb, so it is accusative as a ḥāl concerning them, meaning: remaining therein, ḥaqibīn, jaḥidīn (deprived and denying).

His saying: ﴿لا يذوقون فيها بردا ولا شرابا﴾ (They will not taste therein any coolness or drink) is an explanation of it, and the exception is disjunctive, meaning: they will not taste therein any coolness or refreshment that cools the heat of the fire for them, nor any drink that quenches their thirst; rather, they will taste therein ﴿حميمًا وغسّاقا﴾ (scalding water and dark, cold liquid). End of quote. He had put forward before this view the following text: "It is possible that what is meant is: remaining therein for ages, not tasting coolness or drink except scalding water and dark liquid, then after the ages they will be given in exchange something other than the scalding water and dark liquid, of another kind of punishment." End of quote. This view (p-414) which he stated is an opinion of the earlier scholars, related by Ibn ‘Atiyya. He said: Others said the meaning is: remaining therein for ages, not tasting coolness or drink; in this state they will remain for ages, and then the punishment will continue everlastingly while they drink the drinks of Hell. What appears is that His saying ﴿لا يذوقون﴾ is a new independent sentence and not in the position of a ḥāl, and ﴿إلا حميمًا﴾ is a connected exception from His saying ﴿ولا شرابا﴾, and that ﴿أحقابا﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, following the well-known usage of the Arabic language, not as an accusative of ḥāl according to that less well-known dialect. The saying of whoever said that those described as abiding for ages are the disobedient believers is refuted by the endings of the verses. Muqatil's saying that this is abrogated by His saying ﴿فذوقوا فلن نزيدكم إلا عذابا﴾ is corrupt. The apparent meaning, which is the view of the majority, is that coolness (bard) is the touch of cold air, that is, nothing touches them from it that is pleasant and breaks the intensity of the heat. Abu ‘Ubayda, al-Kisa’i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Mu‘adh al-Nahwi said: bard here means sleep, and the Arabs call it that because it cools the blaze of thirst. From their speech: "Sleep prevented coolness (bard) from cooling." The poet said:
"If you wished, I would forbid women other than you, and if you wished, I would not taste nuqakh or bard (sleep)."
Al-Nuqakh is water, and bard is sleep. In the book Lughat fi'l-Qur'an it is stated that bard is sleep in the dialect of Hudhayl. On these two views the tasting is figurative. Ibn ‘Abbas said: bard is cold, delicious drink, and from it is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:
"They give to drink whoever comes to al-Barisa among them, coolness mixed with a flowing, sealed wine."
And from it is the saying of another:
"Sweet longings from Su‘da, as if Su‘da had given you to drink of them, coolness, when you were thirsty."
On this view, the tasting is literal. The grammarians recite on this view the verse of Hassan: Baradā, with a fatḥa on the rā’ and the dāl, followed by the feminine alif, which is a river in Damascus. The explanation of ḥamīm and ghassāq has already been given, and the readers' difference concerning the shadda and the lightness of the shīn. (وِفاقًا) (wifāqan): that is, corresponding to their deeds and their disbelief. The recompense is described by a verbal noun of wāfaqa, or by omitting a modifier, meaning: possessing correspondence. Al-Farra’ said: it is the plural of wifq. The majority read with a light fā’, while Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya and Ibn Abi ‘Abla read it with a shadda, from waffaqahu kadhā. (لا يرجون) (lā yarjūna): they do not fear, or they do not believe. Expecting and hoping are different, and the meaning here is: they do not affirm reckoning, so they neither believe nor fear. The majority read (كِذّابًا) (kidhdhāban) with a shadda on the dhāl, the verbal noun of kadhdhaba, and this is a dialect of some Yemeni Arabs who make the verbal noun of fa‘ala as fi‘āl, while others make its verbal noun on the pattern tafʿīl, like taktheeb. From that dialect is the saying of the poet:
"Indeed, it has long hindered me from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from my healing."
And from the speech of one of them when he sought a legal ruling: "Is shaving better for you or shortening?" He meant trimming, that is in the Hajj. Al-Zamakhshari said: fi‘āl in the pattern fa‘ala is common in the speech of the eloquent Arabs, who say nothing else; one of them heard me explaining a verse and said: "You have explained it with fisār (explanation), such as has never been heard." ‘Ali, ‘Awf al-A‘rabi, Abu Raja’, al-A‘mash and ‘Isa, with a variant from him, read it with a light dhāl. The companion of al-Lawāmiḥ said: ‘Ali and ‘Isa of Basra and ‘Awf al-A‘rabi: (kidhāban), both with lightness, and that is the dialect of Yemen, by making the verbal noun of kadhiba light, kidhāban, like kataba kitāban, so the verbal noun here carries the meaning of the verb rather than its form, like u‘tīhi ‘aṭā’an. End of quote. Al-A‘sha said:
"So I confirmed her and I denied her, and a man benefits from his lying."
Al-Zamakhshari said: it is like His saying ﴿أنبتكم من الأرض نباتا﴾ [Nuh: 17], meaning: they denied Our signs, so they lied a lie; or you make it accusative by kadhabū, which does not imply the meaning of kadhdhabū, since every one who denies the truth is a liar; and if you make it in the sense of mutual lying, its meaning is: they denied Our signs, so they lied to one another a mutual lying; or they denied them while lying, since when they were liars in the eyes of the Muslims and the Muslims were liars in their eyes, there was mutual lying between them; or because they speak with what is excessive in lying, like one who strives in a matter and reaches the utmost of his effort. End of quote. The first grammatical analysis is the more apparent, and anything else is far-fetched. In the book of Ibn ‘Atiyya and the book of al-Lawāmiḥ: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz read, and in the book of Ibn Khalawayh: ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz and al-Majishun; then they agreed on (كُذّابًا) (kuddhāban) with a ḍamma on the kāf and a shadda on the dhāl. It is explained as the plural of kādhib, accusative as an emphatic ḥāl, or as a singular adjective of a verbal noun, meaning: a denial, lying excessively, excessive in denial. The majority read ﴿وكل شيء﴾ (wa kulla shay’) in the accusative, while Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative. (كِتابًا) (kitāban) is in the accusative as a verbal noun from the meaning of (aḥṣaynāhu), that is, an enumeration; or (aḥṣaynāhu) carries the meaning of (katabnāhu), and the figurative usage is either in the verbal noun or in the verb, because they meet in the meaning of recording; or it is a verbal noun in the position of a ḥāl, or written in the Preserved Tablet and in the scroll of the recording angels. ﴿وكل شيء﴾ is a general term with a specific sense, meaning: every thing that is subject to reward and punishment; and it is a parenthetical sentence. ﴿فذوقوا﴾ (fa-dhūqū) is a consequence of their disbelief in the reckoning, and so of their denial of the signs.

‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar said: No verse was revealed concerning the people of the Fire more severe than this one. Abu Burda related it from the Prophet (ﷺ). When He mentioned some of the state of the people of the Fire, He mentioned what is for the people of Paradise, saying: ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾ (Indeed, for the righteous is a place of success), that is, a place of triumph and victory, where they were removed from the Fire and admitted into Paradise. (حدائق) (ḥadā'iqa) is a substitute for ﴿مفازا﴾ and for (fawzan), so the substance (jirm) substitutes for the meaning with an omission, meaning: the triumph of gardens, that is, by them. (دهاقا) (dihāqan): the majority said: overflowing. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: consecutive. The majority read ﴿ولا كذابا﴾ (wa lā kidhdhāban) with a shadda, meaning: some of them will not lie to others. al-Kisa’i read it with lightness, as in the first word in His saying: ﴿وكذبوا بآياتنا كذابا﴾, the verbal noun of kadhdhaba and the verbal noun of kādhaba. Al-Zamakhshari said: (جزاءً) (jazā'an) is an emphatic verbal noun in the accusative, in the sense of His saying: ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾, as if He said: He recompensed the righteous with triumph and a gift; it is accusative by jazā' as an object, meaning: their recompense is a gift. End of quote. This is not permissible, because he made it an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾, and an emphatic verbal noun does not govern, since it cannot be resolved into a conjunction plus the verb; and we know of no disagreement on that. The majority read (حِسابًا) (ḥisāban), which is an adjective of ‘aṭā’ (gift), meaning sufficient, from their saying: aḥsabanī al-shay’, that is, it sufficed me. Mujahid said: the meaning of ḥisāban here is by distribution according to the deeds, or entry into Paradise by the mercy of God, and the ranks therein are according to the deeds; so the reckoning here is by weighing the deeds. Ibn Qutayb read ḥassāban with a fatḥa on the ḥā’ and a shadda on the sīn. Ibn Jinni said: he formed fa‘‘āl from af‘ala, like darrāk from adraka. End of quote. So its meaning is maḥsib, that is, sufficient. Shurayh ibn Yazid al-Ḥimsi and Abu al-Barahsam read it with a kasra on the ḥā’ and a shadda on the sīn, and it is a verbal noun like kidhdhāb placed in the position of an adjective, that is, a gift that is sufficient (muḥassab), that is, adequate. Ibn ‘Abbas and Sarah read ḥasanan with an nūn, from al-husn (goodness). Al-Mahdawi related from him ḥasban with a fatḥa on the ḥā’ and a sukūn on the sīn and the bā’, like your saying: ḥasbuka kadhā, that is, sufficient for you.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 78, verses 21–40 (part 2 of 2):

Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read (rabbi, wa-l-Rahmani) with the genitive case (jarr) on both. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu 'Amr and the two Haramis read both with the nominative (raf'), while al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read (rabbi) in the genitive and (al-Rahmanu) in the nominative. This is the reading of al-Hasan, Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, and Ibn Muhaysin, with a variant transmitted from the latter two regarding the genitive, as a substitution (badal) from ﴿rabbika﴾. (Al-Rahman) is either an attribute (sifa), or a substitute (badal) from (rabb), or an appositive ('atf bayan). Whether it can be a substitute from ﴿rabbika﴾ is open to question, because an apparent substitute is not repeated, so it would function like the attributes. The nominative is either by supposing (huwa rabbu, "He is the Lord"), or as a new subject (ibtida'), with its predicate being ﴿la yamlikun﴾. The pronoun in ﴿la yamlikun﴾ refers to the polytheists, as said by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, meaning that the polytheists do not address God; as for the believers, they intercede and God accepts that from them. It is also said that it refers to the believers, meaning they do not have the power to address Him concerning any matter, because they know that whatever He does is just. It is also said that it refers to the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, and the pronoun in ﴿minhu﴾ refers to Him, Exalted, and the meaning is that they do not have the power, from God, to address Him concerning anything of reward and punishment with an address by which they could dispose of it as owners do, adding to it or subtracting from it.

The governing element of (yawma) is either ﴿la yamlikun﴾ or ﴿la yatakallamun﴾. The disagreement about (al-Ruh) has already been mentioned: is it Gabriel, or the greatest of the angels in creation, or a creation in the form of the children of Adam, or a creation that guards the angels, or the spirits of the children of Adam, or the Qur'an and its standing? (Qiyam here) is a metaphor, meaning the manifestation of its effects resulting from its confirmation or denial. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿la yatakallamun﴾ refers to ﴿al-Ruh wa-l-mala'ikah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said it refers to the people, so no one speaks except by permission from Him, Exalted, and he speaks what is right. 'Ikrimah said: "what is right" is "there is no god but God," meaning he said it in this world. Al-Zamakhshari said: these are two conditions: that the speaker among them be permitted to speak, and that he speak what is right, so he does not intercede for anyone who is not approved, based on His saying, Exalted: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28]. End of quotation.

﴿That is the true day﴾, meaning its existence and occurrence. ﴿So whoever wills﴾ is a warning and threat. The address in ﴿We have warned you﴾ is to those present with the Prophet (ﷺ), and whoever comes after them is included. (A punishment) is the punishment of the Hereafter, because its occurrence is certain, and everything that is coming is near. ﴿The Day when a man looks at what his hands have sent forward﴾ is general to the believer and the disbeliever, ﴿of good or evil﴾, since proof is established for him and against him. Al-Zamakhshari said, and 'Ata' said before him, that (al-mar') is the disbeliever, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾, and the disbeliever is expressed by an apparent noun placed in the position of the pronoun to increase blame. The meaning of ﴿what his hands have sent forward﴾ is evil, based on His saying: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Anfal: 50], ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Anfal: 51]. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Hasan said: (al-mar') here is the believer, as if they looked at his counterpart in His saying: ﴿and the disbeliever says﴾.

The majority read (al-mar'u) with a fatha on the mim, while Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a damma, and Abu Hatim considered this weak; it should not be considered weak, because it is a dialect in which the vowel of the mim follows the vowel of the hamza, so they say (mur'un), (mar'an), and (mir'in) according to the case endings (i'rab). (Ma) is in the accusative governed by (yandhuru), and its meaning is: he awaits what his hands have sent forward; so (ma) is a relative pronoun. It is also permissible that (yandhuru) be from looking (al-nazar), and it is suspended from the clause, so it is in the position of the accusative by supposing the removal of the preposition. (Ma) is an interrogative, in the accusative, as previously mentioned; and his wish for that is, that he be dust in this world and was never created, or on that day. Abu Hurayrah and Abdullah ibn 'Umar said: God, Exalted, brings the animals on the Day of Resurrection and takes retribution from some of them for others, then says to them after that: "Be dust," and all of them become dust. So when the disbeliever sees that, he wishes for the same. It is also said: the disbeliever here is Iblis, who, when he sees what the believers obtain of reward, says: ﴿O, would that I were dust﴾, like Adam, who was created from dust, and whom he had despised at first. It is also said: (turaban) means humble in obedience to God, Exalted, neither tyrannical nor arrogant.

Al-Zamakhshari said: fi‘āl in the pattern fa‘ala is common in the speech of the eloquent Arabs, who say nothing else; one of them heard me explaining a verse and said: "You have explained it with fisār (explanation), such as has never been heard." ‘Ali, ‘Awf al-A‘rabi, Abu Raja’, al-A‘mash and ‘Isa, with a variant from him, read it with a light dhāl. The companion of al-Lawāmiḥ said: ‘Ali and ‘Isa of Basra and ‘Awf al-A‘rabi: (kidhāban), both with lightness, and that is the dialect of Yemen, by making the verbal noun of kadhiba light, kidhāban, like kataba kitāban, so the verbal noun here carries the meaning of the verb rather than its form, like u‘tīhi ‘aṭā’an. End of quote. Al-A‘sha said:
"So I confirmed her and I denied her, and a man benefits from his lying."
Al-Zamakhshari said: it is like His saying ﴿أنبتكم من الأرض نباتا﴾ [Nuh: 17], meaning: they denied Our signs, so they lied a lie; or you make it accusative by kadhabū, which does not imply the meaning of kadhdhabū, since every one who denies the truth is a liar; and if you make it in the sense of mutual lying, its meaning is: they denied Our signs, so they lied to one another a mutual lying; or they denied them while lying, since when they were liars in the eyes of the Muslims and the Muslims were liars in their eyes, there was mutual lying between them; or because they speak with what is excessive in lying, like one who strives in a matter and reaches the utmost of his effort. End of quote. The first grammatical analysis is the more apparent, and anything else is far-fetched. In the book of Ibn ‘Atiyya and the book of al-Lawāmiḥ: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz read, and in the book of Ibn Khalawayh: ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz and al-Majishun; then they agreed on (كُذّابًا) (kuddhāban) with a ḍamma on the kāf and a shadda on the dhāl. It is explained as the plural of kādhib, accusative as an emphatic ḥāl, or as a singular adjective of a verbal noun, meaning: a denial, lying excessively, excessive in denial. The majority read ﴿وكل شيء﴾ (wa kulla shay’) in the accusative, while Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative. (كِتابًا) (kitāban) is in the accusative as a verbal noun from the meaning of (aḥṣaynāhu), that is, an enumeration; or (aḥṣaynāhu) carries the meaning of (katabnāhu), and the figurative usage is either in the verbal noun or in the verb, because they meet in the meaning of recording; or it is a verbal noun in the position of a ḥāl, or written in the Preserved Tablet and in the scroll of the recording angels. ﴿وكل شيء﴾ is a general term with a specific sense, meaning: every thing that is subject to reward and punishment; and it is a parenthetical sentence. ﴿فذوقوا﴾ (fa-dhūqū) is a consequence of their disbelief in the reckoning, and so of their denial of the signs.

‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar said: No verse was revealed concerning the people of the Fire more severe than this one. Abu Burda related it from the Prophet (ﷺ). When He mentioned some of the state of the people of the Fire, He mentioned what is for the people of Paradise, saying: ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾ (Indeed, for the righteous is a place of success), that is, a place of triumph and victory, where they were removed from the Fire and admitted into Paradise. (حدائق) (ḥadā'iqa) is a substitute for ﴿مفازا﴾ and for (fawzan), so the substance (jirm) substitutes for the meaning with an omission, meaning: the triumph of gardens, that is, by them. (دهاقا) (dihāqan): the majority said: overflowing. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: consecutive. Al-Zamakhshari said: (جزاءً) (jazā'an) is an emphatic verbal noun in the accusative, in the sense of His saying: ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾, as if He said: He recompensed the righteous with triumph and a gift; it is accusative by jazā' as an object, meaning: their recompense is a gift. End of quote. This is not permissible, because he made it an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾, and an emphatic verbal noun does not govern, since it cannot be resolved into a conjunction plus the verb; and we know of no disagreement on that. The majority read (حِسابًا) (ḥisāban), which is an adjective of ‘aṭā’ (gift), meaning sufficient, from their saying: aḥsabanī al-shay’, that is, it sufficed me. Mujahid said: the meaning of ḥisāban here is by distribution according to the deeds, or entry into Paradise by the mercy of God, and the ranks therein are according to the deeds; so the reckoning here is by weighing the deeds. Ibn Qutayb read ḥassāban with a fatḥa on the ḥā’ and a shadda on the sīn. Ibn Jinni said: he formed fa‘‘āl from af‘ala, like darrāk from adraka. End of quote. So its meaning is maḥsib, that is, sufficient. Shurayh ibn Yazid al-Ḥimsi and Abu al-Barahsam read it with a kasra on the ḥā’ and a shadda on the sīn, and it is a verbal noun like kidhdhāb placed in the position of an adjective, that is, a gift that is sufficient (muḥassab), that is, adequate. Ibn ‘Abbas and Sarah read ḥasanan with an nūn, from al-husn (goodness). Al-Mahdawi related from him ḥasban with a fatḥa on the ḥā’ and a sukūn on the sīn and the bā’, like your saying: ḥasbuka kadhā, that is, sufficient for you.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 78, verses 21–40 (part 2 of 2):

Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read (rabbi, wa-l-Rahmani) with the genitive case (jarr) on both. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu 'Amr and the two Haramis read both with the nominative (raf'), while al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read (rabbi) in the genitive and (al-Rahmanu) in the nominative. This is the reading of al-Hasan, Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, and Ibn Muhaysin, with a variant transmitted from the latter two regarding the genitive, as a substitution (badal) from ﴿rabbika﴾. (Al-Rahman) is either an attribute (sifa), or a substitute (badal) from (rabb), or an appositive ('atf bayan). Whether it can be a substitute from ﴿rabbika﴾ is open to question, because an apparent substitute is not repeated, so it would function like the attributes. The nominative is either by supposing (huwa rabbu, "He is the Lord"), or as a new subject (ibtida'), with its predicate being ﴿la yamlikun﴾. The pronoun in ﴿la yamlikun﴾ refers to the polytheists, as said by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, meaning that the polytheists do not address God; as for the believers, they intercede and God accepts that from them. It is also said that it refers to the believers, meaning they do not have the power to address Him concerning any matter, because they know that whatever He does is just. It is also said that it refers to the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, and the pronoun in ﴿minhu﴾ refers to Him, Exalted, and the meaning is that they do not have the power, from God, to address Him concerning anything of reward and punishment with an address by which they could dispose of it as owners do, adding to it or subtracting from it.

The governing element of (yawma) is either ﴿la yamlikun﴾ or ﴿la yatakallamun﴾. The disagreement about (al-Ruh) has already been mentioned: is it Gabriel, or the greatest of the angels in creation, or a creation in the form of the children of Adam, or a creation that guards the angels, or the spirits of the children of Adam, or the Qur'an and its standing? (Qiyam here) is a metaphor, meaning the manifestation of its effects resulting from its confirmation or denial. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿la yatakallamun﴾ refers to ﴿al-Ruh wa-l-mala'ikah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said it refers to the people, so no one speaks except by permission from Him, Exalted, and he speaks what is right. 'Ikrimah said: "what is right" is "there is no god but God," meaning he said it in this world. Al-Zamakhshari said: these are two conditions: that the speaker among them be permitted to speak, and that he speak what is right, so he does not intercede for anyone who is not approved, based on His saying, Exalted: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28]. End of quotation.

﴿That is the true day﴾, meaning its existence and occurrence. ﴿So whoever wills﴾ is a warning and threat. The address in ﴿We have warned you﴾ is to those present with the Prophet (ﷺ), and whoever comes after them is included. (A punishment) is the punishment of the Hereafter, because its occurrence is certain, and everything that is coming is near. ﴿The Day when a man looks at what his hands have sent forward﴾ is general to the believer and the disbeliever, ﴿of good or evil﴾, since proof is established for him and against him. Al-Zamakhshari said, and 'Ata' said before him, that (al-mar') is the disbeliever, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾, and the disbeliever is expressed by an apparent noun placed in the position of the pronoun to increase blame. The meaning of ﴿what his hands have sent forward﴾ is evil, based on His saying: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Anfal: 50], ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Anfal: 51]. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Hasan said: (al-mar') here is the believer, as if they looked at his counterpart in His saying: ﴿and the disbeliever says﴾.

The majority read (al-mar'u) with a fatha on the mim, while Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a damma, and Abu Hatim considered this weak; it should not be considered weak, because it is a dialect in which the vowel of the mim follows the vowel of the hamza, so they say (mur'un), (mar'an), and (mir'in) according to the case endings (i'rab). (Ma) is in the accusative governed by (yandhuru), and its meaning is: he awaits what his hands have sent forward; so (ma) is a relative pronoun. It is also permissible that (yandhuru) be from looking (al-nazar), and it is suspended from the clause, so it is in the position of the accusative by supposing the removal of the preposition. (Ma) is an interrogative, in the accusative, as previously mentioned; and his wish for that is, that he be dust in this world and was never created, or on that day. Abu Hurayrah and Abdullah ibn 'Umar said: God, Exalted, brings the animals on the Day of Resurrection and takes retribution from some of them for others, then says to them after that: "Be dust," and all of them become dust. So when the disbeliever sees that, he wishes for the same. It is also said: the disbeliever here is Iblis, who, when he sees what the believers obtain of reward, says: ﴿O, would that I were dust﴾, like Adam, who was created from dust, and whom he had despised at first. It is also said: (turaban) means humble in obedience to God, Exalted, neither tyrannical nor arrogant.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 78, verse 21–40 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: (p-413) ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lookout,﴾ ﴿a dwelling place for the transgressors,﴾ ﴿remaining therein for ages.﴾ ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or drink,﴾ ﴿except scalding water and dark, cold liquid,﴾ ﴿as a recompense, fitting.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they used not to expect any reckoning,﴾ ﴿and they denied Our signs with [great] denial.﴾ ﴿And We have enumerated all things in writing.﴾ ﴿So taste [this], for We will not increase you except in torment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, for the righteous is a place of success:﴾ ﴿gardens and grapevines,﴾ ﴿and full-breasted companions of equal age,﴾ ﴿and a full cup.﴾ ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk or lying,﴾ ﴿as a reward from your Lord, a gift [in full] calculated,﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Most Merciful; they will not be able to address Him,﴾ ﴿the Day the Spirit and the angels will stand in rows. None will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he will say what is correct.﴾ ﴿That is the Day of Truth. So whoever wills may take to his Lord a return.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment, the Day a man will look at what his hands have put forth, and the disbeliever will say, "Would that I were dust!"﴾.

(مِرْصادًا) (mirṣādan): a lookout. It is on the pattern mif‘āl, from al-raṣd (watching), meaning it watches over whoever the word of punishment has come due upon. Muqatil said: "a place of waiting for the enemies and a passageway for the allies." The form mif‘āl is used for both masculine and feminine without a tā’ and carries the sense of the relative (nisba), i.e., "possessing watching"; and everything that comes in reports and attributes in the sense of nisba carries the sense of intensification and permanence. Al-Azhari said: al-mirṣād is the place where the enemy is watched. Al-Hasan said: "Indeed, over Hell is a lookout: whoever comes with a passport passes, and whoever does not come with a passport is detained." Abu ‘Amr, al-Minqari and Ibn Ya‘mar read ﴿أنّ جهنم﴾ (anna jahannama) with a fatḥa on the hamza, while the majority read it with a kasra. (مَآبًا) (ma’aban): a return. ‘Abdullah, ‘Alqama, Zayd ibn ‘Ali, Ibn Thabbat, ‘Amr ibn Maymun, ‘Amr ibn Shurahbil, Talha, al-A‘mash, Hamza, Qutayba, Sawra and Rawh read ﴿لَبِثِينَ﴾ (labithina) without an alif after the lam, while the majority read it with an alif after it. Fā‘il indicates one in whom the act has occurred, and fa‘il indicates one whose nature is that, like ḥādhir and ḥadhir. (أحْقابًا) (aḥqāban): its discussion has preceded in al-Kahf at His saying: ﴿أو أمضي حقبا﴾ [al-Kahf: 60]. The meaning here is: age after age, each age followed by another without end. The word ḥuqub is used only where the succession of times is intended, as in the verse of Abu Tammam:
"Indeed, the ages have taken from the abode of Mawiyya, the ages that wear down the abandoned places, or are they plundered?"

It is permissible for ﴿للطاغين﴾ (lil-ṭāghīna) to be connected to ﴿مرصادا﴾, and it is permissible for it to be connected to (ma’aban). ﴿لابثين﴾ (lābithīna) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from ﴿الطاغين﴾, and ﴿أحقابا﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time. Al-Zamakhshari said: there is another possibility, that it be from ḥaqiba ‘āmunā when its rain and goodness diminish, and ḥaqiba when one misses sustenance, so he is ḥaqib, and its plural is aḥqāb, so it is accusative as a ḥāl concerning them, meaning: remaining therein, ḥaqibīn, jaḥidīn (deprived and denying).

His saying: ﴿لا يذوقون فيها بردا ولا شرابا﴾ (They will not taste therein any coolness or drink) is an explanation of it, and the exception is disjunctive, meaning: they will not taste therein any coolness or refreshment that cools the heat of the fire for them, nor any drink that quenches their thirst; rather, they will taste therein ﴿حميمًا وغسّاقا﴾ (scalding water and dark, cold liquid). End of quote. He had put forward before this view the following text: "It is possible that what is meant is: remaining therein for ages, not tasting coolness or drink except scalding water and dark liquid, then after the ages they will be given in exchange something other than the scalding water and dark liquid, of another kind of punishment." End of quote. This view (p-414) which he stated is an opinion of the earlier scholars, related by Ibn ‘Atiyya. He said: Others said the meaning is: remaining therein for ages, not tasting coolness or drink; in this state they will remain for ages, and then the punishment will continue everlastingly while they drink the drinks of Hell. What appears is that His saying ﴿لا يذوقون﴾ is a new independent sentence and not in the position of a ḥāl, and ﴿إلا حميمًا﴾ is a connected exception from His saying ﴿ولا شرابا﴾, and that ﴿أحقابا﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, following the well-known usage of the Arabic language, not as an accusative of ḥāl according to that less well-known dialect. The saying of whoever said that those described as abiding for ages are the disobedient believers is refuted by the endings of the verses. Muqatil's saying that this is abrogated by His saying ﴿فذوقوا فلن نزيدكم إلا عذابا﴾ is corrupt. The apparent meaning, which is the view of the majority, is that coolness (bard) is the touch of cold air, that is, nothing touches them from it that is pleasant and breaks the intensity of the heat. Abu ‘Ubayda, al-Kisa’i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Mu‘adh al-Nahwi said: bard here means sleep, and the Arabs call it that because it cools the blaze of thirst. From their speech: "Sleep prevented coolness (bard) from cooling." The poet said:
"If you wished, I would forbid women other than you, and if you wished, I would not taste nuqakh or bard (sleep)."
Al-Nuqakh is water, and bard is sleep. In the book Lughat fi'l-Qur'an it is stated that bard is sleep in the dialect of Hudhayl. On these two views the tasting is figurative. Ibn ‘Abbas said: bard is cold, delicious drink, and from it is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:
"They give to drink whoever comes to al-Barisa among them, coolness mixed with a flowing, sealed wine."
And from it is the saying of another:
"Sweet longings from Su‘da, as if Su‘da had given you to drink of them, coolness, when you were thirsty."
On this view, the tasting is literal. The grammarians recite on this view the verse of Hassan: Baradā, with a fatḥa on the rā’ and the dāl, followed by the feminine alif, which is a river in Damascus. The explanation of ḥamīm and ghassāq has already been given, and the readers' difference concerning the shadda and the lightness of the shīn. (وِفاقًا) (wifāqan): that is, corresponding to their deeds and their disbelief. The recompense is described by a verbal noun of wāfaqa, or by omitting a modifier, meaning: possessing correspondence. Al-Farra’ said: it is the plural of wifq. The majority read with a light fā’, while Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya and Ibn Abi ‘Abla read it with a shadda, from waffaqahu kadhā. (لا يرجون) (lā yarjūna): they do not fear, or they do not believe. Expecting and hoping are different, and the meaning here is: they do not affirm reckoning, so they neither believe nor fear. The majority read (كِذّابًا) (kidhdhāban) with a shadda on the dhāl, the verbal noun of kadhdhaba, and this is a dialect of some Yemeni Arabs who make the verbal noun of fa‘ala as fi‘āl, while others make its verbal noun on the pattern tafʿīl, like taktheeb. From that dialect is the saying of the poet:
"Indeed, it has long hindered me from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from my healing."

It is also said that it refers to the believers, meaning they do not have the power to address Him concerning any matter, because they know that whatever He does is just. It is also said that it refers to the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, and the pronoun in ﴿minhu﴾ refers to Him, Exalted, and the meaning is that they do not have the power, from God, to address Him concerning anything of reward and punishment with an address by which they could dispose of it as owners do, adding to it or subtracting from it.

The governing element of (yawma) is either ﴿la yamlikun﴾ or ﴿la yatakallamun﴾. The disagreement about (al-Ruh) has already been mentioned: is it Gabriel, or the greatest of the angels in creation, or a creation in the form of the children of Adam, or a creation that guards the angels, or the spirits of the children of Adam, or the Qur'an and its standing? (Qiyam here) is a metaphor, meaning the manifestation of its effects resulting from its confirmation or denial. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿la yatakallamun﴾ refers to ﴿al-Ruh wa-l-mala'ikah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said it refers to the people, so no one speaks except by permission from Him, Exalted, and he speaks what is right. 'Ikrimah said: "what is right" is "there is no god but God," meaning he said it in this world. Al-Zamakhshari said: these are two conditions: that the speaker among them be permitted to speak, and that he speak what is right, so he does not intercede for anyone who is not approved, based on His saying, Exalted: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28]. End of quotation.

﴿That is the true day﴾, meaning its existence and occurrence. ﴿So whoever wills﴾ is a warning and threat. The address in ﴿We have warned you﴾ is to those present with the Prophet (ﷺ), and whoever comes after them is included. (A punishment) is the punishment of the Hereafter, because its occurrence is certain, and everything that is coming is near. ﴿The Day when a man looks at what his hands have sent forward﴾ is general to the believer and the disbeliever, ﴿of good or evil﴾, since proof is established for him and against him. Al-Zamakhshari said, and 'Ata' said before him, that (al-mar') is the disbeliever, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾, and the disbeliever is expressed by an apparent noun placed in the position of the pronoun to increase blame. The meaning of ﴿what his hands have sent forward﴾ is evil, based on His saying: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Anfal: 50], ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Anfal: 51]. It is also permissible that (yandhuru) be from looking (al-nazar), and it is suspended from the clause, so it is in the position of the accusative by supposing the removal of the preposition. Abu Hurayrah and Abdullah ibn 'Umar said: God, Exalted, brings the animals on the Day of Resurrection and takes retribution from some of them for others, then says to them after that: "Be dust," and all of them become dust. So when the disbeliever sees that, he wishes for the same. It is also said: the disbeliever here is Iblis, who, when he sees what the believers obtain of reward, says: ﴿O, would that I were dust﴾, like Adam, who was created from dust, and whom he had despised at first. It is also said: (turaban) means humble in obedience to God, Exalted, neither tyrannical nor arrogant.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 78, verse 21–40 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: (p-413) ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lookout,﴾ ﴿a dwelling place for the transgressors,﴾ ﴿remaining therein for ages.﴾ ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or drink,﴾ ﴿except scalding water and dark, cold liquid,﴾ ﴿as a recompense, fitting.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they used not to expect any reckoning,﴾ ﴿and they denied Our signs with [great] denial.﴾ ﴿And We have enumerated all things in writing.﴾ ﴿So taste [this], for We will not increase you except in torment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, for the righteous is a place of success:﴾ ﴿gardens and grapevines,﴾ ﴿and full-breasted companions of equal age,﴾ ﴿and a full cup.﴾ ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk or lying,﴾ ﴿as a reward from your Lord, a gift [in full] calculated,﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Most Merciful; they will not be able to address Him,﴾ ﴿the Day the Spirit and the angels will stand in rows. None will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he will say what is correct.﴾ ﴿That is the Day of Truth. So whoever wills may take to his Lord a return.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment, the Day a man will look at what his hands have put forth, and the disbeliever will say, "Would that I were dust!"﴾.

(مِرْصادًا) (mirṣādan): a lookout. It is on the pattern mif‘āl, from al-raṣd (watching), meaning it watches over whoever the word of punishment has come due upon. Muqatil said: "a place of waiting for the enemies and a passageway for the allies." The form mif‘āl is used for both masculine and feminine without a tā’ and carries the sense of the relative (nisba), i.e., "possessing watching"; and everything that comes in reports and attributes in the sense of nisba carries the sense of intensification and permanence. Al-Azhari said: al-mirṣād is the place where the enemy is watched. Al-Hasan said: "Indeed, over Hell is a lookout: whoever comes with a passport passes, and whoever does not come with a passport is detained." Abu ‘Amr, al-Minqari and Ibn Ya‘mar read ﴿أنّ جهنم﴾ (anna jahannama) with a fatḥa on the hamza, while the majority read it with a kasra. (مَآبًا) (ma’aban): a return. ‘Abdullah, ‘Alqama, Zayd ibn ‘Ali, Ibn Thabbat, ‘Amr ibn Maymun, ‘Amr ibn Shurahbil, Talha, al-A‘mash, Hamza, Qutayba, Sawra and Rawh read ﴿لَبِثِينَ﴾ (labithina) without an alif after the lam, while the majority read it with an alif after it. Fā‘il indicates one in whom the act has occurred, and fa‘il indicates one whose nature is that, like ḥādhir and ḥadhir. (أحْقابًا) (aḥqāban): its discussion has preceded in al-Kahf at His saying: ﴿أو أمضي حقبا﴾ [al-Kahf: 60]. The meaning here is: age after age, each age followed by another without end. The word ḥuqub is used only where the succession of times is intended, as in the verse of Abu Tammam:
"Indeed, the ages have taken from the abode of Mawiyya, the ages that wear down the abandoned places, or are they plundered?"

It is permissible for ﴿للطاغين﴾ (lil-ṭāghīna) to be connected to ﴿مرصادا﴾, and it is permissible for it to be connected to (ma’aban). ﴿لابثين﴾ (lābithīna) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from ﴿الطاغين﴾, and ﴿أحقابا﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time. Al-Zamakhshari said: there is another possibility, that it be from ḥaqiba ‘āmunā when its rain and goodness diminish, and ḥaqiba when one misses sustenance, so he is ḥaqib, and its plural is aḥqāb, so it is accusative as a ḥāl concerning them, meaning: remaining therein, ḥaqibīn, jaḥidīn (deprived and denying).

His saying: ﴿لا يذوقون فيها بردا ولا شرابا﴾ (They will not taste therein any coolness or drink) is an explanation of it, and the exception is disjunctive, meaning: they will not taste therein any coolness or refreshment that cools the heat of the fire for them, nor any drink that quenches their thirst; rather, they will taste therein ﴿حميمًا وغسّاقا﴾ (scalding water and dark, cold liquid). End of quote. He had put forward before this view the following text: "It is possible that what is meant is: remaining therein for ages, not tasting coolness or drink except scalding water and dark liquid, then after the ages they will be given in exchange something other than the scalding water and dark liquid, of another kind of punishment." End of quote. This view (p-414) which he stated is an opinion of the earlier scholars, related by Ibn ‘Atiyya. He said: Others said the meaning is: remaining therein for ages, not tasting coolness or drink; in this state they will remain for ages, and then the punishment will continue everlastingly while they drink the drinks of Hell. What appears is that His saying ﴿لا يذوقون﴾ is a new independent sentence and not in the position of a ḥāl, and ﴿إلا حميمًا﴾ is a connected exception from His saying ﴿ولا شرابا﴾, and that ﴿أحقابا﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, following the well-known usage of the Arabic language, not as an accusative of ḥāl according to that less well-known dialect. The saying of whoever said that those described as abiding for ages are the disobedient believers is refuted by the endings of the verses. Muqatil's saying that this is abrogated by His saying ﴿فذوقوا فلن نزيدكم إلا عذابا﴾ is corrupt. The apparent meaning, which is the view of the majority, is that coolness (bard) is the touch of cold air, that is, nothing touches them from it that is pleasant and breaks the intensity of the heat. Abu ‘Ubayda, al-Kisa’i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Mu‘adh al-Nahwi said: bard here means sleep, and the Arabs call it that because it cools the blaze of thirst. From their speech: "Sleep prevented coolness (bard) from cooling." The poet said:
"If you wished, I would forbid women other than you, and if you wished, I would not taste nuqakh or bard (sleep)."
Al-Nuqakh is water, and bard is sleep. In the book Lughat fi'l-Qur'an it is stated that bard is sleep in the dialect of Hudhayl. On these two views the tasting is figurative. Ibn ‘Abbas said: bard is cold, delicious drink, and from it is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:
"They give to drink whoever comes to al-Barisa among them, coolness mixed with a flowing, sealed wine."
And from it is the saying of another:
"Sweet longings from Su‘da, as if Su‘da had given you to drink of them, coolness, when you were thirsty."
On this view, the tasting is literal. The grammarians recite on this view the verse of Hassan: Baradā, with a fatḥa on the rā’ and the dāl, followed by the feminine alif, which is a river in Damascus. The explanation of ḥamīm and ghassāq has already been given, and the readers' difference concerning the shadda and the lightness of the shīn. (وِفاقًا) (wifāqan): that is, corresponding to their deeds and their disbelief. The recompense is described by a verbal noun of wāfaqa, or by omitting a modifier, meaning: possessing correspondence. Al-Farra’ said: it is the plural of wifq. The majority read with a light fā’, while Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya and Ibn Abi ‘Abla read it with a shadda, from waffaqahu kadhā. (لا يرجون) (lā yarjūna): they do not fear, or they do not believe. Expecting and hoping are different, and the meaning here is: they do not affirm reckoning, so they neither believe nor fear. The majority read (كِذّابًا) (kidhdhāban) with a shadda on the dhāl, the verbal noun of kadhdhaba, and this is a dialect of some Yemeni Arabs who make the verbal noun of fa‘ala as fi‘āl, while others make its verbal noun on the pattern tafʿīl, like taktheeb. From that dialect is the saying of the poet:
"Indeed, it has long hindered me from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from my healing."
And from the speech of one of them when he sought a legal ruling: "Is shaving better for you or shortening?" He meant trimming, that is in the Hajj. Al-Zamakhshari said: fi‘āl in the pattern fa‘ala is common in the speech of the eloquent Arabs, who say nothing else; one of them heard me explaining a verse and said: "You have explained it with fisār (explanation), such as has never been heard." ‘Ali, ‘Awf al-A‘rabi, Abu Raja’, al-A‘mash and ‘Isa, with a variant from him, read it with a light dhāl. The companion of al-Lawāmiḥ said: ‘Ali and ‘Isa of Basra and ‘Awf al-A‘rabi: (kidhāban), both with lightness, and that is the dialect of Yemen, by making the verbal noun of kadhiba light, kidhāban, like kataba kitāban, so the verbal noun here carries the meaning of the verb rather than its form, like u‘tīhi ‘aṭā’an. End of quote. Al-A‘sha said:
"So I confirmed her and I denied her, and a man benefits from his lying."
Al-Zamakhshari said: it is like His saying ﴿أنبتكم من الأرض نباتا﴾ [Nuh: 17], meaning: they denied Our signs, so they lied a lie; or you make it accusative by kadhabū, which does not imply the meaning of kadhdhabū, since every one who denies the truth is a liar; and if you make it in the sense of mutual lying, its meaning is: they denied Our signs, so they lied to one another a mutual lying; or they denied them while lying, since when they were liars in the eyes of the Muslims and the Muslims were liars in their eyes, there was mutual lying between them; or because they speak with what is excessive in lying, like one who strives in a matter and reaches the utmost of his effort. End of quote. The first grammatical analysis is the more apparent, and anything else is far-fetched. In the book of Ibn ‘Atiyya and the book of al-Lawāmiḥ: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz read, and in the book of Ibn Khalawayh: ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz and al-Majishun; then they agreed on (كُذّابًا) (kuddhāban) with a ḍamma on the kāf and a shadda on the dhāl. It is explained as the plural of kādhib, accusative as an emphatic ḥāl, or as a singular adjective of a verbal noun, meaning: a denial, lying excessively, excessive in denial. The majority read ﴿وكل شيء﴾ (wa kulla shay’) in the accusative, while Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative. (كِتابًا) (kitāban) is in the accusative as a verbal noun from the meaning of (aḥṣaynāhu), that is, an enumeration; or (aḥṣaynāhu) carries the meaning of (katabnāhu), and the figurative usage is either in the verbal noun or in the verb, because they meet in the meaning of recording; or it is a verbal noun in the position of a ḥāl, or written in the Preserved Tablet and in the scroll of the recording angels. ﴿وكل شيء﴾ is a general term with a specific sense, meaning: every thing that is subject to reward and punishment; and it is a parenthetical sentence. ﴿فذوقوا﴾ (fa-dhūqū) is a consequence of their disbelief in the reckoning, and so of their denial of the signs.

‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar said: No verse was revealed concerning the people of the Fire more severe than this one. Abu Burda related it from the Prophet (ﷺ). When He mentioned some of the state of the people of the Fire, He mentioned what is for the people of Paradise, saying: ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾ (Indeed, for the righteous is a place of success), that is, a place of triumph and victory, where they were removed from the Fire and admitted into Paradise. (حدائق) (ḥadā'iqa) is a substitute for ﴿مفازا﴾ and for (fawzan), so the substance (jirm) substitutes for the meaning with an omission, meaning: the triumph of gardens, that is, by them. (دهاقا) (dihāqan): the majority said: overflowing. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: consecutive. The majority read ﴿ولا كذابا﴾ (wa lā kidhdhāban) with a shadda, meaning: some of them will not lie to others. al-Kisa’i read it with lightness, as in the first word in His saying: ﴿وكذبوا بآياتنا كذابا﴾, the verbal noun of kadhdhaba and the verbal noun of kādhaba. Al-Zamakhshari said: (جزاءً) (jazā'an) is an emphatic verbal noun in the accusative, in the sense of His saying: ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾, as if He said: He recompensed the righteous with triumph and a gift; it is accusative by jazā' as an object, meaning: their recompense is a gift. End of quote. This is not permissible, because he made it an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾, and an emphatic verbal noun does not govern, since it cannot be resolved into a conjunction plus the verb; and we know of no disagreement on that. The majority read (حِسابًا) (ḥisāban), which is an adjective of ‘aṭā’ (gift), meaning sufficient, from their saying: aḥsabanī al-shay’, that is, it sufficed me. Mujahid said: the meaning of ḥisāban here is by distribution according to the deeds, or entry into Paradise by the mercy of God, and the ranks therein are according to the deeds; so the reckoning here is by weighing the deeds. Ibn Qutayb read ḥassāban with a fatḥa on the ḥā’ and a shadda on the sīn. Ibn Jinni said: he formed fa‘‘āl from af‘ala, like darrāk from adraka. End of quote. So its meaning is maḥsib, that is, sufficient. Shurayh ibn Yazid al-Ḥimsi and Abu al-Barahsam read it with a kasra on the ḥā’ and a shadda on the sīn, and it is a verbal noun like kidhdhāb placed in the position of an adjective, that is, a gift that is sufficient (muḥassab), that is, adequate. Ibn ‘Abbas and Sarah read ḥasanan with an nūn, from al-husn (goodness). Al-Mahdawi related from him ḥasban with a fatḥa on the ḥā’ and a sukūn on the sīn and the bā’, like your saying: ḥasbuka kadhā, that is, sufficient for you.

Fā‘il indicates one in whom the act has occurred, and fa‘il indicates one whose nature is that, like ḥādhir and ḥadhir. (أحْقابًا) (aḥqāban): its discussion has preceded in al-Kahf at His saying: ﴿أو أمضي حقبا﴾ [al-Kahf: 60]. The meaning here is: age after age, each age followed by another without end. The word ḥuqub is used only where the succession of times is intended, as in the verse of Abu Tammam:
"Indeed, the ages have taken from the abode of Mawiyya, the ages that wear down the abandoned places, or are they plundered?"

It is permissible for ﴿للطاغين﴾ (lil-ṭāghīna) to be connected to ﴿مرصادا﴾, and it is permissible for it to be connected to (ma’aban). ﴿لابثين﴾ (lābithīna) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from ﴿الطاغين﴾, and ﴿أحقابا﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time. Al-Zamakhshari said: there is another possibility, that it be from ḥaqiba ‘āmunā when its rain and goodness diminish, and ḥaqiba when one misses sustenance, so he is ḥaqib, and its plural is aḥqāb, so it is accusative as a ḥāl concerning them, meaning: remaining therein, ḥaqibīn, jaḥidīn (deprived and denying).

His saying: ﴿لا يذوقون فيها بردا ولا شرابا﴾ (They will not taste therein any coolness or drink) is an explanation of it, and the exception is disjunctive, meaning: they will not taste therein any coolness or refreshment that cools the heat of the fire for them, nor any drink that quenches their thirst; rather, they will taste therein ﴿حميمًا وغسّاقا﴾ (scalding water and dark, cold liquid). End of quote. He had put forward before this view the following text: "It is possible that what is meant is: remaining therein for ages, not tasting coolness or drink except scalding water and dark liquid, then after the ages they will be given in exchange something other than the scalding water and dark liquid, of another kind of punishment." End of quote. This view (p-414) which he stated is an opinion of the earlier scholars, related by Ibn ‘Atiyya. He said: Others said the meaning is: remaining therein for ages, not tasting coolness or drink; in this state they will remain for ages, and then the punishment will continue everlastingly while they drink the drinks of Hell. What appears is that His saying ﴿لا يذوقون﴾ is a new independent sentence and not in the position of a ḥāl, and ﴿إلا حميمًا﴾ is a connected exception from His saying ﴿ولا شرابا﴾, and that ﴿أحقابا﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, following the well-known usage of the Arabic language, not as an accusative of ḥāl according to that less well-known dialect. The saying of whoever said that those described as abiding for ages are the disobedient believers is refuted by the endings of the verses. Muqatil's saying that this is abrogated by His saying ﴿فذوقوا فلن نزيدكم إلا عذابا﴾ is corrupt. The apparent meaning, which is the view of the majority, is that coolness (bard) is the touch of cold air, that is, nothing touches them from it that is pleasant and breaks the intensity of the heat. Abu ‘Ubayda, al-Kisa’i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Mu‘adh al-Nahwi said: bard here means sleep, and the Arabs call it that because it cools the blaze of thirst. From their speech: "Sleep prevented coolness (bard) from cooling." The poet said:
"If you wished, I would forbid women other than you, and if you wished, I would not taste nuqakh or bard (sleep)."
Al-Nuqakh is water, and bard is sleep. In the book Lughat fi'l-Qur'an it is stated that bard is sleep in the dialect of Hudhayl. On these two views the tasting is figurative. Ibn ‘Abbas said: bard is cold, delicious drink, and from it is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:
"They give to drink whoever comes to al-Barisa among them, coolness mixed with a flowing, sealed wine."
And from it is the saying of another:
"Sweet longings from Su‘da, as if Su‘da had given you to drink of them, coolness, when you were thirsty."
On this view, the tasting is literal. The grammarians recite on this view the verse of Hassan: Baradā, with a fatḥa on the rā’ and the dāl, followed by the feminine alif, which is a river in Damascus. The explanation of ḥamīm and ghassāq has already been given, and the readers' difference concerning the shadda and the lightness of the shīn. (وِفاقًا) (wifāqan): that is, corresponding to their deeds and their disbelief. The recompense is described by a verbal noun of wāfaqa, or by omitting a modifier, meaning: possessing correspondence. Al-Farra’ said: it is the plural of wifq. The majority read with a light fā’, while Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya and Ibn Abi ‘Abla read it with a shadda, from waffaqahu kadhā. (لا يرجون) (lā yarjūna): they do not fear, or they do not believe. Expecting and hoping are different, and the meaning here is: they do not affirm reckoning, so they neither believe nor fear. The majority read (كِذّابًا) (kidhdhāban) with a shadda on the dhāl, the verbal noun of kadhdhaba, and this is a dialect of some Yemeni Arabs who make the verbal noun of fa‘ala as fi‘āl, while others make its verbal noun on the pattern tafʿīl, like taktheeb. From that dialect is the saying of the poet:
"Indeed, it has long hindered me from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from my healing."
And from the speech of one of them when he sought a legal ruling: "Is shaving better for you or shortening?" He meant trimming, that is in the Hajj. Al-Zamakhshari said: fi‘āl in the pattern fa‘ala is common in the speech of the eloquent Arabs, who say nothing else; one of them heard me explaining a verse and said: "You have explained it with fisār (explanation), such as has never been heard." ‘Ali, ‘Awf al-A‘rabi, Abu Raja’, al-A‘mash and ‘Isa, with a variant from him, read it with a light dhāl. The companion of al-Lawāmiḥ said: ‘Ali and ‘Isa of Basra and ‘Awf al-A‘rabi: (kidhāban), both with lightness, and that is the dialect of Yemen, by making the verbal noun of kadhiba light, kidhāban, like kataba kitāban, so the verbal noun here carries the meaning of the verb rather than its form, like u‘tīhi ‘aṭā’an. End of quote. Al-A‘sha said:
"So I confirmed her and I denied her, and a man benefits from his lying."
Al-Zamakhshari said: it is like His saying ﴿أنبتكم من الأرض نباتا﴾ [Nuh: 17], meaning: they denied Our signs, so they lied a lie; or you make it accusative by kadhabū, which does not imply the meaning of kadhdhabū, since every one who denies the truth is a liar; and if you make it in the sense of mutual lying, its meaning is: they denied Our signs, so they lied to one another a mutual lying; or they denied them while lying, since when they were liars in the eyes of the Muslims and the Muslims were liars in their eyes, there was mutual lying between them; or because they speak with what is excessive in lying, like one who strives in a matter and reaches the utmost of his effort. End of quote. The first grammatical analysis is the more apparent, and anything else is far-fetched. In the book of Ibn ‘Atiyya and the book of al-Lawāmiḥ: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz read, and in the book of Ibn Khalawayh: ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz and al-Majishun; then they agreed on (كُذّابًا) (kuddhāban) with a ḍamma on the kāf and a shadda on the dhāl. It is explained as the plural of kādhib, accusative as an emphatic ḥāl, or as a singular adjective of a verbal noun, meaning: a denial, lying excessively, excessive in denial. The majority read ﴿وكل شيء﴾ (wa kulla shay’) in the accusative, while Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative. (كِتابًا) (kitāban) is in the accusative as a verbal noun from the meaning of (aḥṣaynāhu), that is, an enumeration; or (aḥṣaynāhu) carries the meaning of (katabnāhu), and the figurative usage is either in the verbal noun or in the verb, because they meet in the meaning of recording; or it is a verbal noun in the position of a ḥāl, or written in the Preserved Tablet and in the scroll of the recording angels. ﴿وكل شيء﴾ is a general term with a specific sense, meaning: every thing that is subject to reward and punishment; and it is a parenthetical sentence. ﴿فذوقوا﴾ (fa-dhūqū) is a consequence of their disbelief in the reckoning, and so of their denial of the signs.

‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar said: No verse was revealed concerning the people of the Fire more severe than this one. Abu Burda related it from the Prophet (ﷺ). When He mentioned some of the state of the people of the Fire, He mentioned what is for the people of Paradise, saying: ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾ (Indeed, for the righteous is a place of success), that is, a place of triumph and victory, where they were removed from the Fire and admitted into Paradise. (حدائق) (ḥadā'iqa) is a substitute for ﴿مفازا﴾ and for (fawzan), so the substance (jirm) substitutes for the meaning with an omission, meaning: the triumph of gardens, that is, by them. (دهاقا) (dihāqan): the majority said: overflowing. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: consecutive. The majority read ﴿ولا كذابا﴾ (wa lā kidhdhāban) with a shadda, meaning: some of them will not lie to others. al-Kisa’i read it with lightness, as in the first word in His saying: ﴿وكذبوا بآياتنا كذابا﴾, the verbal noun of kadhdhaba and the verbal noun of kādhaba. Al-Zamakhshari said: (جزاءً) (jazā'an) is an emphatic verbal noun in the accusative, in the sense of His saying: ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾, as if He said: He recompensed the righteous with triumph and a gift; it is accusative by jazā' as an object, meaning: their recompense is a gift. End of quote. This is not permissible, because he made it an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence ﴿إن للمتقين مفازا﴾, and an emphatic verbal noun does not govern, since it cannot be resolved into a conjunction plus the verb; and we know of no disagreement on that. The majority read (حِسابًا) (ḥisāban), which is an adjective of ‘aṭā’ (gift), meaning sufficient, from their saying: aḥsabanī al-shay’, that is, it sufficed me. Mujahid said: the meaning of ḥisāban here is by distribution according to the deeds, or entry into Paradise by the mercy of God, and the ranks therein are according to the deeds; so the reckoning here is by weighing the deeds. Ibn Qutayb read ḥassāban with a fatḥa on the ḥā’ and a shadda on the sīn. Ibn Jinni said: he formed fa‘‘āl from af‘ala, like darrāk from adraka. End of quote. So its meaning is maḥsib, that is, sufficient. Shurayh ibn Yazid al-Ḥimsi and Abu al-Barahsam read it with a kasra on the ḥā’ and a shadda on the sīn, and it is a verbal noun like kidhdhāb placed in the position of an adjective, that is, a gift that is sufficient (muḥassab), that is, adequate. Ibn ‘Abbas and Sarah read ḥasanan with an nūn, from al-husn (goodness). Al-Mahdawi related from him ḥasban with a fatḥa on the ḥā’ and a sukūn on the sīn and the bā’, like your saying: ḥasbuka kadhā, that is, sufficient for you.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 78, verses 21–40 (part 2 of 2):

Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read (rabbi, wa-l-Rahmani) with the genitive case (jarr) on both. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu 'Amr and the two Haramis read both with the nominative (raf'), while al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read (rabbi) in the genitive and (al-Rahmanu) in the nominative. This is the reading of al-Hasan, Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, and Ibn Muhaysin, with a variant transmitted from the latter two regarding the genitive, as a substitution (badal) from ﴿rabbika﴾. (Al-Rahman) is either an attribute (sifa), or a substitute (badal) from (rabb), or an appositive ('atf bayan). Whether it can be a substitute from ﴿rabbika﴾ is open to question, because an apparent substitute is not repeated, so it would function like the attributes. The nominative is either by supposing (huwa rabbu, "He is the Lord"), or as a new subject (ibtida'), with its predicate being ﴿la yamlikun﴾. The pronoun in ﴿la yamlikun﴾ refers to the polytheists, as said by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, meaning that the polytheists do not address God; as for the believers, they intercede and God accepts that from them. It is also said that it refers to the believers, meaning they do not have the power to address Him concerning any matter, because they know that whatever He does is just. It is also said that it refers to the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, and the pronoun in ﴿minhu﴾ refers to Him, Exalted, and the meaning is that they do not have the power, from God, to address Him concerning anything of reward and punishment with an address by which they could dispose of it as owners do, adding to it or subtracting from it.

The governing element of (yawma) is either ﴿la yamlikun﴾ or ﴿la yatakallamun﴾. The disagreement about (al-Ruh) has already been mentioned: is it Gabriel, or the greatest of the angels in creation, or a creation in the form of the children of Adam, or a creation that guards the angels, or the spirits of the children of Adam, or the Qur'an and its standing? (Qiyam here) is a metaphor, meaning the manifestation of its effects resulting from its confirmation or denial. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿la yatakallamun﴾ refers to ﴿al-Ruh wa-l-mala'ikah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said it refers to the people, so no one speaks except by permission from Him, Exalted, and he speaks what is right. 'Ikrimah said: "what is right" is "there is no god but God," meaning he said it in this world. Al-Zamakhshari said: these are two conditions: that the speaker among them be permitted to speak, and that he speak what is right, so he does not intercede for anyone who is not approved, based on His saying, Exalted: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28]. End of quotation.

﴿That is the true day﴾, meaning its existence and occurrence. ﴿So whoever wills﴾ is a warning and threat. The address in ﴿We have warned you﴾ is to those present with the Prophet (ﷺ), and whoever comes after them is included. (A punishment) is the punishment of the Hereafter, because its occurrence is certain, and everything that is coming is near. ﴿The Day when a man looks at what his hands have sent forward﴾ is general to the believer and the disbeliever, ﴿of good or evil﴾, since proof is established for him and against him. Al-Zamakhshari said, and 'Ata' said before him, that (al-mar') is the disbeliever, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾, and the disbeliever is expressed by an apparent noun placed in the position of the pronoun to increase blame. The meaning of ﴿what his hands have sent forward﴾ is evil, based on His saying: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Anfal: 50], ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Anfal: 51]. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Hasan said: (al-mar') here is the believer, as if they looked at his counterpart in His saying: ﴿and the disbeliever says﴾.

The majority read (al-mar'u) with a fatha on the mim, while Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a damma, and Abu Hatim considered this weak; it should not be considered weak, because it is a dialect in which the vowel of the mim follows the vowel of the hamza, so they say (mur'un), (mar'an), and (mir'in) according to the case endings (i'rab). (Ma) is in the accusative governed by (yandhuru), and its meaning is: he awaits what his hands have sent forward; so (ma) is a relative pronoun. It is also permissible that (yandhuru) be from looking (al-nazar), and it is suspended from the clause, so it is in the position of the accusative by supposing the removal of the preposition. (Ma) is an interrogative, in the accusative, as previously mentioned; and his wish for that is, that he be dust in this world and was never created, or on that day. Abu Hurayrah and Abdullah ibn 'Umar said: God, Exalted, brings the animals on the Day of Resurrection and takes retribution from some of them for others, then says to them after that: "Be dust," and all of them become dust. So when the disbeliever sees that, he wishes for the same. It is also said: the disbeliever here is Iblis, who, when he sees what the believers obtain of reward, says: ﴿O, would that I were dust﴾, like Adam, who was created from dust, and whom he had despised at first. It is also said: (turaban) means humble in obedience to God, Exalted, neither tyrannical nor arrogant.

None will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he will say what is correct.﴾ ﴿That is the Day of Truth.
